newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian police seize rebel explosives cache.
newsitem.headline: Colombian police seize rebel explosives cache.

text.p: Colombia police raided a guerrilla safe house on Thursday and seized 880 pounds (400 kgs) of high explosives destined for a "wave of terrorist attacks" around Bogota, the authorities said.

A police spokesman said plans found in the house in a southern neighbourhood of the capital indicated that National Liberation Army (ELN) rebels intended to target gasoline storage depots and military communications facilities.
"This police operation has averted a new wave of terrorist attacks in the capital," the spokesman said.
Among other documents found were instructions handed down from the ELN leadership to insurgents, ordering them to step up the creation of urban guerrilla cells.

In the last month, the ELN, a Cuban-inspired force set up by radical Roman Catholic priests in the 1960s, has been blamed for two car bomb attacks in eastern Colombia cities that killed a baby and injured dozens of others.

The army also believe the ELN and the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), the country's oldest and largest guerrilla army, jointly planned another car bomb attack in the northwest town of Apartado in February, which killed 11 and wounded more than 60 others.
In another development, Colombian right-wing paramilitaries have freed five kidnapped relatives of the country's top guerrilla chieftains, police said.

The three women and two men were handed over by the so-called Peasant Self-Defence Group of Cordoba and Uraba (ACCU), Colombia's most-feared paramilitary force, to members of the Red Cross and the Dutch human rights group Pax Christi in the northwest province of Cordoba.

All were abducted by the paramilitary force last year as part of a tit-for-tat strategy to force Colombia's Marxist rebels to end their tactic of kidnapping civilians to fill their war chests with ransom payments.
Among those released was Ricardo Saenz, brother of Alfonso Cano, a national leader of the FARC.

"They told us this was a goodwill gesture. We just hope (the FARC) now release the soldiers because there is no argument that justifies kidnapping. It is inhuman," Saenz told the Radionet radio network, referring to the 60 soldiers the FARC took prisoner in an attack on a military base in southern Colombia last August.
